triage.name: Colonic Polyps
triage.reason: Often asymptomatic but reachable via screening history and colonoscopy; good case for screening and cancer-risk counseling.

demographics: Incidence rises steadily with age; most polyps are found on screening colonoscopy in adults over 45

risk_factors.text: Personal history of colonic polyps or prior colorectal cancer
Family history of colorectal cancer or polyps in a first-degree relative
Inherited syndromes such as familial adenomatous polyposis or Lynch syndrome
Inflammatory bowel disease, especially long-standing ulcerative colitis
Diet high in red or processed meat and low in fiber, fruits and vegetables

Colonic polyps in a first-degree relative
social_history: Low fiber or high processed-meat diet

chief_complaints.text: I actually feel fine — I just came in for my colonoscopy screening
I saw a little blood on the toilet paper after I went
My bowels have been off for a couple of weeks
My doctor said my stool test was positive

hpi.onset: Insidious; polyps grow slowly over years and usually cause no symptoms until they are large
hpi.duration: Present for years before detection; symptoms, when they occur, are typically present for days to weeks
hpi.progression: Most polyps are found incidentally at screening and never cause symptoms. Larger or distal polyps may gradually produce intermittent rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habit.
hpi.location: Colon; bleeding is often from the left colon or rectum, while right-sided polyps are more often silent
hpi.quality: Bleeding is typically small in amount and intermittent; bowel changes are described as looser or harder stools than usual
hpi.severity: Mild; most patients feel entirely well
hpi.timing: Bleeding may be noticed only after a bowel movement; bowel changes are persistent rather than episodic

associated_symptoms.text: No symptoms at all — found on routine screening
Small amounts of bright red blood on toilet paper or in the stool
Constipation or diarrhea lasting more than a week
A feeling of incomplete emptying after a bowel movement

pertinent_negatives: Large-volume rectal bleeding or blood mixed throughout the stool

positives.text: Blood on toilet paper or in the stool
Constipation or diarrhea lasting more than a week

argues_against: Bleeding disorder or significant chronic blood loss

atypical.how_it_differs: More likely to have larger, right-sided or advanced polyps, and anemia from occult blood loss may be the only clue.

atypical.how_it_differs: Associated with a higher prevalence of adenomas and a modestly increased risk of progression, but the presentation is still usually asymptomatic.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; often entirely normal
general.moderate: Well-appearing but may look mildly pale if there has been chronic occult blood loss
general.severe: Pale or fatigued appearance suggesting anemia from chronic bleeding; still usually not acutely ill
general.critical: Rarely ill-appearing; consider a complication such as obstruction or perforation rather than the polyp itself

labs.caveat: Most polyps cause no bleeding; anemia is more likely with large or multiple polyps and suggests chronic occult blood loss. A normal hemoglobin does not exclude a polyp.
Low MCV supports iron deficiency from chronic blood loss; check ferritin to confirm.
Low ferritin in an adult with iron deficiency anemia warrants evaluation of the colon even without visible bleeding.
Reactive thrombocytosis can accompany chronic iron deficiency.

decision_points: Colonoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic: polyps are removed at the time of detection and sent for histology.
A positive stool-based screening test (FIT or stool DNA) requires diagnostic colonoscopy regardless of symptoms.
Iron deficiency anemia in an adult over 45 warrants evaluation of the colon even without visible bleeding.
If colonoscopy is incomplete or contraindicated, CT colonography is the next structural test.
Patients with a strong family history or features of a hereditary syndrome (early onset, many polyps, extracolonic findings) need genetic counseling and earlier, more frequent surveillance.

criteria.name: USPSTF colorectal cancer screening
criteria.summary: Screening for colorectal cancer is recommended in all adults aged 45 to 75 years. For adults 76 to 85, the decision is individualized based on overall health and prior screening. Screening may be done with colonoscopy every 10 years, CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or annual FIT, among other options.

criteria.name: Post-polypectomy surveillance intervals
criteria.summary: Surveillance colonoscopy intervals after polypectomy are based on the number, size and histology of the removed polyps. Low-risk findings (1 to 2 small tubular adenomas) generally lead to a 7- to 10-year interval, while high-risk findings (advanced adenomas, 3 or more adenomas, or sessile serrated lesions) shorten the interval to about 3 years.

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: A malignant lesion can present as a polypoid mass and is the main reason polyps are removed and sent for histology.
differential.trigger: Iron deficiency anemia, unintentional weight loss, or a large, friable, or malignant-appearing lesion at colonoscopy

history: Unintentional weight loss
Persistent change in bowel habit over weeks
Blood mixed throughout the stool rather than just on the surface
Family history of colorectal cancer
exam: Supraclavicular or other lymphadenopathy in advanced disease
labs: Iron deficiency anemia with low ferritin
Elevated CEA (not diagnostic, used for monitoring)
imaging: Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated, friable, or circumferential mass rather than a smooth mucosal protrusion
CT or MRI shows invasion beyond the bowel wall or nodal or distant disease

differential.name: Diverticular disease
differential.why_considered: A common cause of intermittent bright red rectal bleeding in older adults, the same symptom that can prompt evaluation for polyps.

history: Known diverticulosis
Painless or mildly painful episodes of bleeding
Left lower quadrant discomfort with fever if diverticulitis
exam: Left lower quadrant tenderness in diverticulitis
imaging: Colonoscopy shows diverticula (outpouchings) rather than protruding polyps
CT shows colonic wall thickening and pericolonic fat stranding in diverticulitis

differential.name: Hemorrhoids
differential.why_considered: A very common cause of bright red blood on toilet paper after a bowel movement, which is also a presenting symptom of distal polyps.

history: Bleeding is typically painless and occurs after defecation
Associated with straining, constipation, or prolonged sitting
No change in bowel habit
exam: Visible external hemorrhoids or prolapsing internal hemorrhoids on inspection
Digital rectal exam may be normal or reveal a tender perianal mass
labs: Usually normal; anemia is uncommon unless bleeding is chronic and heavy
imaging: Colonoscopy shows no polyps; hemorrhoids are seen on anoscopy or external inspection

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Can cause diarrhea, mucus in the stool, and rectal bleeding, and long-standing ulcerative colitis increases polyp and cancer risk.

history: Chronic or recurrent diarrhea, often with urgency and tenesmus
Mucus or blood mixed with stool
Weight loss, fever, or extraintestinal symptoms such as joint pain or rash
Younger age at onset
exam: Perianal fistulas or tags in Crohn disease
imaging: Colonoscopy shows continuous mucosal inflammation, friability, erosions, or pseudopolyps rather than discrete polyps
Biopsy shows chronic inflammation or crypt architectural distortion

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: A common cause of chronic constipation or diarrhea and a change in bowel habit, which can overlap with symptoms attributed to polyps.

history: Chronic relapsing abdominal pain related to defecation
Alternating constipation and diarrhea
No rectal bleeding, weight loss, or anemia
Symptoms often triggered by stress or certain foods
labs: Normal CBC, CRP, and celiac serology
imaging: Colonoscopy normal; no polyps or inflammation

differential.name: Angiodysplasia
differential.why_considered: A vascular cause of intermittent, often occult, lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults, which can mimic bleeding from a polyp.

history: Intermittent bleeding, often in older adults with aortic stenosis or chronic kidney disease
No change in bowel habit
May present with iron deficiency anemia
labs: Normal platelet count and coagulation studies
imaging: Colonoscopy shows flat, red, ectatic vascular lesions rather than protruding polyps
CT angiography or tagged red blood cell scan may localize bleeding if active

severity.mild: Small, asymptomatic polyp found incidentally at screening; no anemia, no bowel habit change, patient feels well.
severity.moderate: Larger or multiple polyps causing intermittent occult bleeding with mild iron deficiency anemia or a persistent change in bowel habit, but no obstruction or systemic symptoms.
severity.severe: Large or advanced polyp with significant anemia, or a polyp that is difficult to remove endoscopically and requires referral or piecemeal resection; still no acute complication.
severity.critical: Rare; a polyp itself is not life-threatening, but a large lesion can cause obstruction, perforation, or massive bleeding, or the polyp may harbor invasive cancer.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests malignancy or advanced disease rather than a benign polyp

red_flags.finding: Iron deficiency anemia in an adult over 45
red_flags.meaning: Requires evaluation of the colon for a bleeding polyp or cancer

red_flags.finding: Large-volume rectal bleeding or blood mixed throughout the stool
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a more proximal or larger bleeding source, possibly malignant

red_flags.finding: Persistent change in stool caliber or pencil-thin stools
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a large obstructing distal lesion
Suggests obstruction from a large polyp or mass

red_flags.finding: Fever, peritoneal signs, or hemodynamic instability after polypectomy

Post-polypectomy bleeding
clues: Rectal bleeding within days after colonoscopy
Use of anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents

complications.name: Colonic obstruction
clues: Inability to pass stool or gas

special_populations.differences: More likely to have larger, right-sided, or advanced polyps; anemia from occult blood loss may be the only clue. Screening decisions should account for overall health and life expectancy.
Higher risk of multiple and advanced polyps; screening may start earlier or be repeated more often.
Associated with a higher prevalence of adenomas and a modestly increased risk of progression, but presentation is still usually asymptomatic.
Colonoscopy is generally deferred to the second trimester if needed; sigmoidoscopy may be preferred for left-sided symptoms. Polyps are usually managed after delivery unless malignancy is suspected.
Higher risk of complications from colonoscopy and polypectomy; consider antibiotic prophylaxis and closer monitoring.

key_questions.question: When was your last colonoscopy, and what did it show?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior polyps or prior colorectal cancer; establishes personal history and surveillance interval

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had colon polyps or colon cancer? How old were they when it was found?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relative with colorectal cancer or polyps, especially before age 60; suggests hereditary risk and earlier screening

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any blood on the toilet paper, in the stool, or on your underwear?
key_questions.looking_for: Intermittent small-volume bright red bleeding, the most common symptom when polyps cause symptoms

key_questions.question: Have your bowel habits changed in the last few weeks?
key_questions.looking_for: Constipation or diarrhea lasting more than a week, or a persistent change from baseline

key_questions.question: Have you had any weight loss, fevers, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms that argue against a benign polyp and raise concern for malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you been told you are anemic, or have you felt unusually tired or short of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Iron deficiency anemia from chronic occult blood loss

key_questions.question: Have you had a stool test for colon cancer screening, and was it positive?
key_questions.looking_for: Positive FIT or stool DNA test, which requires diagnostic colonoscopy

key_questions.question: Do you have any history of inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing colitis, which increases polyp and cancer risk

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol, or eat a lot of red or processed meat?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable risk factors that support the diagnosis and guide counseling

key_questions.question: Are you taking any blood thinners or antiplatelet medications?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulants or antiplatelets that affect polypectomy planning and bleeding risk

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a colonoscopy that could not be completed?
key_questions.looking_for: Incomplete colonoscopy, which may require CT colonography or repeat attempt

reasoning_points: Most colonic polyps are asymptomatic and found incidentally at screening colonoscopy
When symptoms occur, they are usually intermittent small-volume bright red rectal bleeding or a persistent change in bowel habit
Age over 45, personal history of polyps or colorectal cancer, and family history of colorectal cancer or polyps are the strongest risk factors
Physical examination is typically normal; a digital rectal exam may show gross blood but usually no palpable mass
Iron deficiency anemia in an adult over 45 warrants evaluation of the colon even without visible bleeding
Colonoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic: polyps are removed at detection and sent for histology
A positive stool-based screening test (FIT or stool DNA) requires diagnostic colonoscopy regardless of symptoms
Surveillance intervals after polypectomy depend on the number, size, and histology of the removed polyps
Features suggesting a hereditary syndrome (early onset, many polyps, extracolonic findings) require genetic counseling and earlier, more frequent surveillance
